stem: Why can relatively small changes in upper-airway calibre matter more in infants than in adults?

options.text: A compliant chest wall gives more support to lung volume
Respiratory tract infections are usually bacterial
A large occiput increases oxygen offload to tissues

explanation: Smaller diameter airways increase resistance. In infants, a small reduction in airway calibre produces a proportionally larger rise in resistance, so minor narrowing has a bigger clinical effect.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Respiratory 3.1 Acute Respiratory Problems

rationale: Infants have smaller airways, so resistance rises more steeply when calibre decreases.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because a compliant chest wall provides less support for maintenance of lung volume, not more.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because fewer alveoli relate to gas exchange and V/Q mismatch, not lower airway resistance.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because paediatric respiratory tract infections are usually acute viral infections, not usually bacterial.
optionExplanations.D: Correct because smaller airway diameter increases resistance, so even small narrowing can significantly increase work of breathing in infants.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because a large occiput affects head position and airway patency, not oxygen offload to tissues.

sourceRefs: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
